note: The ceremony profiles. scripts/regen-ceremony-profiles.py generates
the Solidity, Rust and TypeScript constants from this file, and the
hand-written Platform Verifiers read them.
These literals are this repository's: REQ-PLAT-01 fixes the profile
names and the specification fixes no other byte. The verifiers, the
browser that notarizes the sessions and the notary must produce the
same bytes. A mismatch fails silently: a Consumer and a verifier keyed
by different strings never meet, and a request line composed one byte
differently is refused with no reason given.
Changing a value changes what a deployed verifier accepts. On a live
deployment that is a new ceremonyVersion; a fresh deployment keeps its
versions.
Header names no notarized request may carry, compared lowercased, with
whitespace removed and `_` read as `-`. Each changes what the platform
does in a way no revealed byte shows: `authorization` the client it
authenticates, `content-encoding` and `transfer-encoding` the bytes it
parses, `cookie` the session, the three override names the method. The
identity request is excepted from `authorization` alone: its one such
header, under any scheme, is what REQ-COMMON-39 counts. The verifier
also requires each session's requiredHeaders once with their value,
reads the token request's `content-length`, and ignores every other
header: such a header changes only the response, which the verifier
then cannot read.
Google's evidence is a token signed with Google's published keys, so
the profile notarizes nothing: no session, no attestation and no
Notary Fee.
The signed `exp` bounds validity, so the profile fixes no lifetime and
no attestation skew. The OIDC circuit exposes no `iat`, so the
observation is the token's `exp`, about an hour after Google issued
it.
A public client with S256 PKCE and two browser-owned sessions, both
served by the same host.
The token attestation's creation time is the evidence time. A notary
states the wall-clock time it observes, so five minutes covers clock
skew between the notary and the chain.
A public client hides no body field: the request is revealed whole and
the verifier accepts zero committed ranges in this direction.
The media type is required because it decides how X parses the bytes
the verifier reads as a form. REQ-COMMON-21B fixes it in the
deployment profile because it selects the platform's request parser.
requiredHeaders are the head lines the verifier requires, each once
with its value. Other headers the browser or a client sends are not
compared, except requests.forbiddenHeaders. The HTTP client appends
`content-length`, and the verifier checks it against the length the
notary signed.
tokenFields is the specification's X order, and the verifier holds the
whole body to it: these five, in order, each once with a nonempty
value in the serializer's one spelling, and nothing more
(REQ-PLAT-63). A form X might read as a sixth field, such as a raw `;`
in a value, an encoded name or a second `grant_type`, is refused, so
acceptance does not rest on ASM-PROV-07. The verifier reads three
values: `code_verifier`, which the digest recomputes; `client_id`,
held to REQ-COMMON-16B's charset; and `grant_type`, compared to
`authorization_code` (REQ-PLAT-56).
X's id is a JSON string, so both members are read by their full
`"field":"` delimiters.
The credential GitHub calls `client_secret` is sent and revealed, so
an attestation publishes it. The two sessions are served by different
hosts, so each session pins its own authority.

validity.note: Same as X: notary wall-clock, five minutes for skew.

note: The request is revealed whole, credential included, so the verifier
accepts zero committed ranges in this direction.
The media type, section 6.2's, is required because it decides how
GitHub parses the bytes the verifier reads as a form. `host` names the
authority the notary authenticated. The client also sends `accept:
application/json`, without which GitHub answers form-encoded and the
verifier finds no `"access_token":"`, and `connection: close`, which
ends the session. Neither is compared.
tokenFields is what the verifier holds the whole body to: these five,
in order, each once with a nonempty value in the serializer's one
spelling, and nothing more (REQ-PLAT-61). A form GitHub might read as
a sixth field, such as a raw `;` in a value, an encoded name or a
`grant_type`, is refused, so acceptance does not rest on ASM-PROV-07.
The verifier reads `code_verifier`, which the digest recomputes, and
`client_id`, held to REQ-COMMON-16B's charset, and no other value.
GitHub's id is a bare integer, read with its terminator pinned to `,`
or `}`: the terminator proves the revealed digits are the whole number
(REQ-PLAT-51).
